directive: Valerius continues his political correspondence while resolving the disputed boundary by purchasing the land rather than prolonging the argument, with spring administration and the existing raid inquiry continuing around the estate.

events.title: VALERIUS'S POLITICAL CORRESPONDENCE CONTINUES INTO THE SPRING
events.body: A new exchange connected with Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer reaches Valerius as the winter correspondence gives way to the spring season. The letter concerns the earlier matters already placed before the Roman political circle and asks for several points to be clarified without requiring Valerius to travel immediately. Valerius answers through his scribes and keeps the reply measured, distinguishing what he personally witnessed from what had been reported to him by others. Copies of the correspondence are retained with the estate papers so that later questions can be answered from the same record. The exchange adds another layer to Valerius's growing political correspondence without creating a formal office or public appointment. His name continues to circulate among Roman correspondents while the estate remains the center from which he conducts the exchange.

events.title: THE DISPUTED BOUNDARY IS SETTLED BY AGREEMENT TO PURCHASE
events.body: After reviewing the statements and older descriptions assembled during February, Valerius chooses not to continue arguing over the disputed tract. He meets with the affected smallholders and offers to purchase the land in question at an agreed price rather than leave the neighboring households in a continuing boundary dispute. The owners accept the proposal, and the parties arrange for the sale to be entered into the estate's ordinary property records with the boundaries described clearly enough to prevent the same disagreement from immediately returning. The transaction concerns a small tract of roughly forty acres and does not involve the seizure of any neighboring property. Payment is made from the estate's operating capital, and the sellers depart with the dispute settled by contract rather than by a contested ruling. The purchase gives Valerius a modest addition to his holdings while ending a local quarrel that had been growing more complicated.

events.title: THE PURCHASE BRINGS AN EARLY END TO THE NEIGHBORING PROPERTY DISPUTE
events.body: News of the purchase spreads through the nearby settlement before the new property description has even been copied into every relevant estate book. Several of the households that had joined the petition return to confirm that the disputed access and boundary question will no longer require a prolonged hearing. The former disagreement is replaced by practical questions about the new boundary markers, the path used by neighboring farmers, and the terms under which the existing road remains open. Valerius instructs his stewards to have those details written down rather than leaving the settlement to rely on verbal assurances. The change is notable because the dispute ends without a public judgment declaring one side correct and the other wrong. What had threatened to become a recurring local quarrel is instead converted into an ordinary property transaction and a clearer administrative boundary.

events.title: MARCELLUS RECEIVES ANOTHER RESPONSE FROM VALERIUS
events.body: Valerius sends another response to Marcus Claudius Marcellus after the questions that occupied the estate library during the winter. The reply includes several local interpretations and preserves the disagreements between the readers instead of presenting them as a single authoritative conclusion. Marcellus's earlier interest in the estate's discussions has therefore developed into a continuing correspondence rather than a single exchange of letters. Valerius's scribes make a copy before the original is sent and place it with the other Roman correspondence. The political and intellectual strands of his correspondence remain distinct, but both continue to bring the estate into contact with people beyond its immediate district. The spring correspondence consequently begins with the same deliberate habit of record-keeping that characterized the winter.

events.title: THE NEWLY PURCHASED TRACT IS MARKED FOR SPRING USE
events.body: Once the purchase papers have been entered into the estate records, stewards begin marking the newly acquired tract for its first spring use. The work is deliberately limited at first, with boundary points checked against the descriptions agreed in the sale and the existing route left usable for neighboring farmers. Workers clear the portions that can be brought into ordinary cultivation without interfering with the newly settled boundary. The former owners remain involved in identifying the landmarks described in the agreement, reducing the chance that an old field memory will later contradict the written sale. No large construction project begins on the tract. Its immediate significance lies in turning a disputed piece of ground into a clearly administered part of the estate.

events.title: THE RAID CORRESPONDENCE PRODUCES ANOTHER REQUEST FOR RECORDS
events.body: Another communication concerning the earlier raid inquiry arrives before the month closes. The request seeks clarification on the sequence of testimony already preserved in Valerius's papers and asks that the supporting copies remain together with the original chronology. Valerius has the estate scribes retrieve the relevant papers and compare them against the copies previously sent through the correspondence. Aulus Vettius remains present in the documentary chain, but the new request does not establish a fresh accusation against him. The matter therefore remains an inquiry built around records and testimony rather than a new confrontation in the field. Valerius's continuing correspondence gives the Roman side of the matter a fuller documentary trail as spring begins.

events.title: MARCH CLOSES WITH THE DISPUTED LAND NOW PART OF THE ESTATE
events.body: By the end of March the disputed tract has passed from a contested boundary matter into an ordinary entry in Valerius's property records. The purchase deed, payment record, boundary description, and notes concerning the continued use of the neighboring path are placed together in the estate archive. The stewards begin treating the land as part of the regular holding while keeping the agreement available in case any of the neighboring households later asks to inspect it. At the same time, Valerius's political correspondence continues, and the raid inquiry remains active through written exchanges rather than public confrontation. The estate therefore enters April with a new piece of land, a settled local dispute, and several continuing Roman connections. The purchase has changed the administrative situation without requiring force, confiscation, or a ruling against the people who originally disputed the boundary.
